records.title: Fukushima Daiichi treated water still flowing into the Pacific in its fourth year, with China's seafood ban only partly lifted
records.description: Japan began releasing ALPS-treated water from the Fukushima Daiichi plant on 24 August 2023 under a roughly 30-year plan. By the start of the 21st round on 6 July 2026, about 157,000 tonnes had been discharged, and the IAEA's on-site analysis has found tritium far below the 1,500 Bq per litre operational limit. China banned all Japanese seafood in 2023 and partly lifted the ban on 29 June 2025, still excluding Tokyo, Fukushima and eight other prefectures.

location.name: Fukushima Daiichi discharge, Pacific coast
location.detail: Futaba, Fukushima Prefecture, Tohoku, Japan; treated water is released through a seawater tunnel off the plant's Pacific shore

records.layer_rationale: Controlled release of tritiated water from a damaged nuclear plant into the sea, with trade and monitoring consequences.

notes.harm: The IAEA found tritium in the diluted water far below the 1,500 Bq per litre operational limit, so no exceedance is documented, but each round releases about 1.3 trillion Bq of tritium (refs 1, 4).
notes.livelihoods: Japanese seafood exports to China fell 99.3% year on year in September 2023 from a pre-ban value of about JPY75bn, and Tokyo, Fukushima and eight other prefectures remain excluded after the June 2025 partial lifting (refs 2, 3).
notes.scale: Discharges run from one plant on the Fukushima coast but affect national fishery markets and regional trade, which we score as a national coastline (refs 3, 4).
notes.duration: Releases began on 24 August 2023 and continue under a roughly 30-year plan, with eight rounds and about 62,400 tonnes planned for fiscal 2026 (refs 1, 4).
notes.significance: China's customs authority imposed a blanket import ban on release day and Russia joined the restrictions; the IAEA monitors every batch and a China-Japan monitoring accord followed in September 2024 (refs 1, 2, 5).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Kuroshio Extension meander gave Japan's Sanriku coast two years of record warming, about 6 degrees C above normal
records.description: Sea surface temperature off the Sanriku coast ran about 6 degrees C above normal from February 2023 to January 2025 while the Kuroshio Extension meandered far north, which the University of Tokyo's Atmosphere and Ocean Research Institute calls the most intense warming in the world's oceans. Warm-water fish appeared off Miyagi for the first time and fishers report poor catches, and Japan's Meteorological Agency declared the larger Kuroshio meander over in August 2025.

location.name: Sanriku coast and Kuroshio Extension
location.detail: Pacific coast of Tohoku (Aomori, Iwate, Miyagi), reaching south to the Boso and Kanto coasts

records.layer_rationale: Persistent marine heatwave driven by a shifted western boundary current.

notes.harm: Warm-water cardinalfish and southern yellowtail were confirmed off Miyagi for the first time, the warming reached about 700 m depth, and kombu harvests are declining sharply (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: Mie Gaiwan fishers report mackerel catches at 20 to 30 percent of ten years ago, and Sanriku salmon and saury became harder to catch, but no closure is documented (ref 2).
notes.scale: The anomaly covered the Pacific coast of Japan's Tohoku region and the Kuroshio Extension, a national coastline (ref 1).
notes.duration: Temperatures stayed about 6 C above normal from February 2023 to January 2025, and marine heatwave conditions were present almost daily from April 2023 to August 2024 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The Japan Meteorological Agency formally declared the large meander ended in August 2025 and linked the ocean state to record 2023 summer heat, backed by a peer-reviewed study (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Derelict nets and plastic keep arriving in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands: 72,150 lb removed in 2025 and about 49,000 lb in 2026
records.description: The Papahānaumokuākea Marine Debris Project removed 72,150 pounds of marine debris from Pearl and Hermes Atoll and Kure Atoll in September and October 2025, and cleared about 49,000 pounds on its 2026 voyage. The project says it has removed more than 1.2 million pounds over six years, and a 2022 report put new accumulation at about 57 tons a year.

location.detail: Northwestern Hawaiian Islands including Pearl and Hermes Atoll, Kure Atoll and Laysan Island, Hawaii, United States

records.layer_rationale: Ocean currents deliver lost fishing gear and plastic to a remote protected reef system.

notes.harm: Nets and trash accumulate on reefs and shorelines of a protected monument and the project's 2025 season targeted nets with drones and undersea scooters, but no mortality figure is given for 2025 or 2026 (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: The cited reports describe no fishery, tourism or access restriction linked to the debris (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: Work spanned several atolls across the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands, including Pearl and Hermes, Kure and Laysan, which we score as a national coastline (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The project has removed more than 1.2 million pounds over six years and an estimated 57 tons accumulate on the reefs each year (refs 2, 3).
notes.significance: Removal is run by a nonprofit project and a 2025 hack-a-thon, with no formal notice, enforcement or listing described in the cited sources (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Runit Dome nuclear waste cap on Enewetak Atoll exposed to rising seas, GAO and DOE reports find
records.description: The Runit Dome in the Marshall Islands holds contaminated soil and debris from US nuclear weapons tests in an unlined crater under a non-load-bearing concrete cap. GAO reported in January 2024 that Marshallese officials fear rising seas may affect contaminated sites and that DOE has struggled to explain its view that the health risk is low, and DOE's July 2024 report to Congress found storm surge with sea-level rise would matter most. A March 2026 report describes cracks in the cap and groundwater entering the crater.

location.name: Runit Dome, Enewetak Atoll
location.detail: Runit Island, Enewetak Atoll, northern Marshall Islands; Runit is off limits and about 275 people live on Enewetak Island

records.layer_rationale: Radioactive waste from nuclear tests contained at sea level on a coral atoll, with leaching and sea-level risk.

notes.harm: DOE's modelled doses stay below 0.1 mrem per year with the dome intact and below 0.2 mrem per year after a hypothetical failure, so harm is potential; a 2026 report notes groundwater already enters the unlined crater (refs 2, 3).
notes.livelihoods: Runit Island is indefinitely off limits, and only Enewetak Island, about 275 people, is inhabited; the Marshallese government disputes DOE's low-risk view (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The dome is a single containment structure on one island, although lagoon sediments across the atoll hold most of the long-term radioactivity (ref 2).
notes.duration: The dome was built in the late 1970s and DOE's study projects conditions to 2090 with 62 cm of sea-level rise, so the exposure is chronic (ref 2).
notes.significance: GAO issued formal report GAO-24-104082 whose communication recommendation remained open in July 2026, and DOE delivered a statutory report to Congress (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: Only Enewetak Island, about 13 miles from Runit, is inhabited, by roughly 275 people (ref 2).

key_measure.text: DOE's modelled change in dose is below 0.1 mrem per year with the dome intact and below 0.2 mrem per year after a hypothetical 2090 failure, on islands other than Runit (ref 2).

records.title: Open North Pacific acidifying faster below the surface near Hawaii and steadily across the western subtropical gyre
records.description: A University of Hawaii study of 35 years of Hawaii Ocean Time-series data at Station ALOHA, about 60 miles north of Oahu, found that acidification is faster below the surface than at the surface for every indicator, from the surface to nearly 3 miles deep. Japan's Meteorological Agency reports surface pH falling about 0.02 per decade along 137E and 165E, close to the global rate, and 0.016 to 0.029 per decade in the interior at 150 to 800 m.

location.name: North Pacific subtropical gyre (Station ALOHA, 137E, 165E)
location.detail: Station ALOHA north of Oahu, Hawaii, and Japan Meteorological Agency repeat sections along 137E (3N to 34N) and 165E (5S to 35N)

records.layer_rationale: Absorption of atmospheric carbon dioxide is changing seawater carbonate chemistry across the water column.

notes.harm: The University of Hawaii release says more acidic deep water could harm plankton and other organisms below the surface, but it reports no documented mortality (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: None of the cited sources report a fishery, aquaculture or access effect from open-ocean acidification here (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.scale: JMA's sections span 3N to 35N along 137E and 165E and the Hawaii record covers the whole water column, a basin-scale signal (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The Station ALOHA record is 35 years, JMA's 137E series starts in 1985 and its 165E series in 1996, and trends continue (refs 1, 2, 4).
notes.significance: These are research and agency monitoring results without a formal notice, listing or enforcement, so the score is 0 (refs 1, 2, 3).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Surface pH is falling about 0.02 per decade along JMA's 137E and 165E lines, almost the same as the global ocean, and faster below the surface near Hawaii (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Great Pacific Garbage Patch holds about 100,000 tonnes of plastic over 1.6 million sq km, and cleanup has removed a fraction
records.description: The Ocean Cleanup estimates the patch between Hawaii and California covers about 1.6 million square kilometres and holds about 100,000 tonnes of plastic, mostly fishing gear. By April 2024 it had verifiably removed over 345,000 kg in 18 trips, about a third of a percent, and in July 2026 it said it would test drone-guided steering in the patch on a six-week expedition.

location.name: Great Pacific Garbage Patch
location.detail: North Pacific subtropical gyre between Hawaii and California, centred on average near 32N 145W

records.layer_rationale: Floating plastic concentrated by the gyre's circulation.

notes.harm: The Ocean Cleanup estimates about 1.8 trillion pieces and about 100,000 tonnes of plastic, of which fishing nets were 46% of the mass in 2018, but no mortality count is given in these pages (refs 1, 4).
notes.livelihoods: The cited pages describe no fishery, shipping or tourism restriction from the patch (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.scale: The patch spans about 1.6 million square kilometres of the high seas in the North Pacific subtropical gyre, which is basin scale (ref 4).
notes.duration: Plastic has accumulated since the 2018 survey and the first cleanup extraction in 2019, with removal continuing through 2026 (refs 1, 2, 4).
notes.significance: The estimates come from a nonprofit and a peer-reviewed 2018 study and no formal notice, listing or treaty action on the patch is described in the cited pages (refs 1, 4).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Apra Harbor, Guam, logged a record 77 high-tide flood days in 2025-26, and Hawaii's Kawaihae and Hilo 44 each
records.description: NOAA's 2026-27 outlook review reports that Apra Harbor, Guam, set a station record of 77 high-tide flood days in the 2025-26 meteorological year against a predicted 4 to 11, which NOAA attributes to elevated regional sea levels. In Hawaii, Kawaihae and Hilo each had 44 flood days and all but one Hawaiian station saw more flooding than predicted, while Honolulu's 15 days were within its range.

records.layer_rationale: Sea-level rise and elevated regional water levels raise the frequency of tidal flooding.

notes.harm: NOAA counts days above the minor flood threshold, which it describes as typically low threat of property damage, and notes true flood days may be fewer, so harm is potential (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The NOAA outlook documents flood-day counts only and cites no closure, displacement or port disruption (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The 2025-26 flooding spans Guam, Hawaii and Wake Island gauges across the Western and Central Pacific, scored as national coastlines (ref 1).
notes.duration: The Pacific Islands are predicted to average 13 more flood days per year than in 2000, a nearly 750% increase, so the problem is chronic and rising (ref 1).
notes.significance: NOAA's formal annual outlook records a new station record at Apra Harbor and an above-normal 2026 Central Pacific hurricane season forecast, but no emergency declaration is cited (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Majuro and the Marshall Islands face frequent flooding, with 96% of the capital at risk and Kwajalein forecast 22 to 43 flood days
records.description: A World Bank and Marshall Islands government study found 40 percent of buildings in the capital Majuro endangered and 96 percent of the city facing frequent climate-linked flooding. GAO reported in 2024 that Marshallese officials worry rising seas may affect contaminated sites, and NOAA's 2026-27 outlook predicts 22 to 43 high-tide flood days at Kwajalein, though NOAA warns its flood threshold may not represent Kwajalein.

notes.duration: The World Bank study models the next 100 years and NOAA's 2026-27 outlook forecasts continuing high-tide flooding at Kwajalein (refs 1, 3).
notes.significance: A formal government and World Bank assessment and a GAO report record the exposure, but no emergency declaration or inundation event for 2024 to 2026 was found (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Pacific saury stock stays far below past levels as the NPFC trims quotas by only 5% for 2026
records.description: Japan's saury landings fell from about 300,000 tons until 2009 to about 18,000 tons in 2022. records.title: US court halts commercial fishing reopened in Pacific Islands Heritage monument waters
records.description: After an April 2025 presidential proclamation, the National Marine Fisheries Service told permit holders they could fish 50 to 200 nautical miles around Johnston Atoll, Jarvis Island and Wake Island. In early August 2025 a federal judge in Hawaii granted environmental and Native Hawaiian plaintiffs' motion, and boats catching fish for sale were required to stop. records.title: HMNZS Manawanui wreck and diesel spill on the reef off Upolu, Samoa
records.description: The New Zealand Navy survey ship HMNZS Manawanui grounded on the reef off Upolu's south coast on 5 October 2024 and sank the next day with an estimated 900,000 or more litres of diesel aboard. Local authorities estimated about 200,000 litres leaked in the first week, salvors later removed more than 300,000 litres of diesel and the wreck remains on the reef, with a court martial and an environmental assessment still pending in 2026.

records.layer_rationale: Fuel oil released from a grounded and sunk naval vessel onto a fringing reef.

notes.harm: About 200,000 litres of diesel leaked in the first week and the ship travelled about 400 yards over the reef; Safata village leaders say shores, reef and mangroves were damaged, although SROS tests found seawater uncontaminated (refs 2, 4, 6).
notes.livelihoods: A precautionary fishing zone was imposed after the sinking and later lifted, but a no-go zone around the wreck still blocks fishing, and one resident says about 80% of locals depend on the sea for food (refs 2, 4).
notes.scale: The documented damage is confined to one reef and the Safata coast of Upolu (refs 3, 4).
notes.duration: The grounding was in October 2024 and the wreck was still on the reef, with the environmental report under stakeholder review, in October 2025 and a fuel sheen checked in February 2026 (refs 1, 5).
notes.significance: A Navy court of inquiry blamed human error, Samoa's Cabinet decided the wreck stays, New Zealand agreed compensation, and charges were laid in the Court Martial of New Zealand on 2 March 2026 (refs 1, 4, 6).

records.title: Funafuti reclamation races rising seas as over half of Tuvalu is forecast to flood regularly by 2050
records.description: Sea levels around Tuvalu rose about 15 cm in the three decades to 2023, roughly twice the global average, according to NASA researchers cited by Reuters in October 2026. Donor-funded work worth about US$50 million is building sea walls and raising land on Funafuti, with about 21 hectares planned, while NASA flood maps project that areas with fewer than five high-tide flood days a year could average 25 by the 2050s.

records.layer_rationale: Sea-level rise and tidal flooding threaten a low-lying atoll nation.

notes.harm: Reuters reports about 15 cm of sea-level rise in three decades and a further 30 cm expected by 2050, and the prime minister cites forecasts of regular tidal flooding of over 50% of land by 2050, so harm is potential rather than documented loss (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: The cited sources document no closure or displacement; they describe sea walls and barriers to protect schools, clinics and crops from storm surges (ref 2).
notes.scale: The whole country's land area is affected, a national coastline rather than a single site (refs 2, 3).
notes.duration: The 15 cm rise accumulated over the three decades to 2023 and the reclamation programme spans phases from 2023 to a 2026 target (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: NASA ran the flood analysis at the request of Tuvalu and Kiribati with the US State Department, and donor-funded adaptation works are formally under way, but no enforcement action applies (refs 3, 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Serua Island, Fiji: king-tide flooding and erosion leave a chiefly village facing relocation
records.description: WMO's 2025 South-West Pacific report describes how, since 2000, higher king tides and seawater intrusion have destroyed Serua Island's seawall, submerged homes and killed food crops, and on two occasions the island could be crossed by boat. Fiji's government has offered relocation support, but most of the roughly 150 residents are choosing to stay because of ties to ancestral land.

records.title: Lomaiviti Princess II sinks in Suva Harbour and leaks oil as 17 derelict vessels await removal
records.description: The abandoned passenger ferry Lomaiviti Princess II capsized and sank in Suva Harbour in early June 2025 after being towed from Narain Jetty, releasing oil that responders contained with booms and dispersants. A joint maritime committee found its owner had not defuelled it despite removal notices, and Fiji has funded a multi-phase clean-up of 17 high-risk derelict vessels expected to run into 2026.

notes.harm: Oil leaked into the harbour and dispersants were applied to minimise harm to marine life, but the volume spilled is not stated and a Ministry of Environment chemical analysis was still to be done (refs 1, 3).
notes.livelihoods: The wreck rests in just under two metres of water, a hazard to navigation in the channel, and Fiji Ports towed it to clear wharf space (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The spill and the derelict hulks are confined to Suva Harbour (refs 4, 5).
notes.duration: The vessel had been abandoned since 2019, the spill response was set for four to eight weeks, and the derelict clean-up is expected to run into 2026 (refs 3, 5).
notes.significance: The Joint Maritime Environment Committee found breaches of the Maritime Transport Act 2013 (section 129) and the minister ordered a full investigation, with penalties of up to FJ$1 million or three years cited, and Cabinet approved a review of the MSAF Act (refs 1, 3, 5).

records.title: Moruroa and Fangataufa nuclear test atolls: lagoon contamination and compensation remain disputed
records.description: France tested 193 nuclear devices at Moruroa and Fangataufa from 1966 to 1996 and dumped an estimated 3,200 tonnes of radioactive waste in Polynesian waters. France says continuing sampling shows no abnormalities and that IAEA experts saw no need for remediation, while a January 2026 National Assembly amendment states that lagoon sediments still show elevated contamination and the atolls remain defence nuclear installations.

records.title: Record 2024 sea-surface temperatures and nearly 40 million km2 of marine heatwaves across the South-West Pacific
records.description: WMO's South-West Pacific report, released on 5 June 2025, says ocean warming in 2024 reached unprecedented levels, with record sea-surface temperatures, near-record ocean heat content and nearly 40 million km2 affected by marine heatwaves, the largest area since 1993. The report says strongest warming over five decades is in the Tasman and Solomon Seas and around the Pacific small island states.

records.layer_rationale: Record ocean heat and marine heatwaves across a wide Pacific region.

notes.harm: WMO says ocean heat and acidification combined to inflict long-lasting damage on marine ecosystems and economies, without a counted loss in the cited text (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: The cited pages record no fishery closure or advisory tied to the heatwaves (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.scale: Nearly 40 million km2, more than 10% of the global ocean surface, was affected by marine heatwaves (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: 2024 was the highest sea-surface temperature on record and the strongest ocean warming of the past five decades is around the Pacific small island states (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: A formal WMO regional State of the Climate report, with warming described as unprecedented (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Ocean acidification monitoring around Pacific island nations remains patchy as regional pH falls
records.description: WMO reports that the entire South-West Pacific ocean area is acidifying, with average surface pH falling 0.017 per decade over 1985 to 2023. The Pacific Community's ocean science centre said in 2023 that monitoring around island nations is patchy and that regional data are scarce, and it has been supplying low-cost pH and temperature loggers to nine Pacific countries since 2021, with a trial site in Suva harbour.

location.detail: South-West Pacific region; the Pacific Islands Ocean Acidification Centre is based in Suva, Fiji, and trialled loggers in Suva harbour; nine other Pacific countries were supplied with devices but are not named.

records.layer_rationale: Falling seawater pH with limited monitoring coverage in island waters.

notes.harm: WMO says ocean heat and acidification combined to inflict long-lasting damage on marine ecosystems, with the pH decline measured at 0.017 per decade; no organism-specific loss is cited (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: No closure, advisory or fishery loss is attributed to acidification in the cited sources (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.scale: WMO says the entire ocean area of the South-West Pacific region is acidifying (ref 2).
notes.duration: The pH change is measured over 1985 to 2023 and the monitoring gap was still described in 2023 and 2025 (refs 2, 3).
notes.significance: A formal WMO regional report documents the trend, while the monitoring network is a capacity programme rather than an enforcement or treaty action (refs 1, 3).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: On average for the region, surface pH decreased by 0.017 plus or minus 0.001 per decade over 1985 to 2023 (WMO, 2025).

records.title: Extreme high tides and record rain flood Tongatapu's low-lying coast in October 2024
records.description: Tonga Met reported that extreme high tides on 18 and 19 October 2024 inundated coastal areas of Tongatapu and 'Eua, damaging infrastructure and homes, alongside the highest October daily rainfall ever recorded in Tonga. A consultant risk assessment describes Nuku'alofa as about two metres above sea level with sea level rising 6.4 mm a year over the past decade.

location.detail: Popua, Fasi, Fanga, Ma'ufanga, Ngele'ia, Pili and Fanga-o-Pilolevu on Tongatapu were among the flooded areas; 'Eua was also affected.

notes.harm: Heavy rain and extreme high tides on 18 to 19 October inundated coastal areas, damaging infrastructure and homes, with no casualty figure in the report (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Apifo'ou College was still flooded four days after the rain (ref 1).
notes.scale: Named neighbourhoods on Tongatapu and 'Eua, a local rather than national-coastline event (ref 1).
notes.duration: The tidal flooding lasted days, while the consultant study records sea level rising 6.4 mm a year for a decade, so exposure recurs (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Tonga Met issued a formal statement on the flooding and the record rainfall, and published sea-level outlooks of 30 to 60 mm above average for southern Tonga to February 2025 (ref 1).

records.title: Henderson Island, Pitcairn Islands: world's densest recorded beach plastic, with a UNESCO-backed clean-up in 2024
records.description: A 2017 PNAS survey estimated 37.7 million debris items weighing 17.6 tons on Henderson Island's beaches, the highest density recorded anywhere, with up to 26.8 new items per metre of beach arriving daily. A 2019 expedition removed about six tonnes and Plastic Odyssey and UNESCO ran a further clean-up in February 2024, with no newer survey found.

records.title: ITLOS Seabed Disputes Chamber orders the ISA to observe due process in its inquiry into Nauru- and Tonga-sponsored contractors NORI and TOML
records.description: On 18 July 2026 the Seabed Disputes Chamber of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea unanimously prescribed provisional measures in two cases (Cases 34 and 35) brought by Nauru Ocean Resources Inc. (NORI) and Tonga Offshore Mining Ltd. (TOML) against the International Seabed Authority. The Chamber did not suspend the Authority's inquiry into possible contractual non-compliance; it ordered the Authority to act within the legal framework, including due process, in the inquiry and in the extension of NORI's exploration contract, and to clarify procedures and questions to the contractor. The Nauru government reported that the ISA Council approved a five-year extension of NORI's contract on 20 July 2026.

location.name: ISA exploration contracts sponsored by Nauru and Tonga
location.detail: International waters of the Pacific administered by the ISA; the case was heard in Hamburg and concerns ISA Council decisions taken in Kingston, Jamaica. NORI is sponsored by Nauru and TOML by Tonga (refs 1, 4).

records.layer_rationale: A court-ordered dispute between two sponsored mining contractors and the seabed regulator over how compliance inquiries are run.

notes.harm: The cited sources describe a procedural dispute over an inquiry; no environmental harm from exploration or mining is reported in the ITLOS or ISA texts (refs 1, 3).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery, community or livelihood disruption is reported in the court or ISA documents on the case (refs 1, 3).
notes.scale: Two contracts sponsored by two Pacific states (Nauru and Tonga) are in dispute, with implications for the wider ISA contractor regime (refs 1, 5).
notes.duration: The inquiry stems from a Council decision of 21 July 2025 and reached the Chamber in June 2026, so it has run for about a year (ref 1).
notes.significance: The Chamber delivered unanimous provisional-measures orders on 18 July 2026 in its first contentious proceedings, which is a tribunal ruling (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure applies to this governance dispute.

key_measure.text: The Chamber ordered the ISA to act in accordance with the legal framework, including due process, in the inquiry and in the NORI contract extension, with compliance reports due 31 August 2026 (ref 2).

records.title: US company applies to NOAA for a seabed mineral exploration licence in the South Penrhyn Basin high seas near Kiribati, the Cook Islands and French Polynesia

NOAA held a virtual hearing on 1 July 2026 and took comments to 3 August 2026. The Pacific Islands Climate Action Network (PICAN) urged public submissions, noting that the US domestic route proceeds while the ISA has yet to finalise rules for commercial mining in international waters.

records.title: Cook Islands extends seabed minerals exploration to 2032 as a NOAA survey, US and China ties and public opposition shape the mining debate
records.description: The Cook Islands government says no decision to mine has been made, and Cook Islands News reported in November 2025 that exploration would be extended five years, pushing any mining decision to at least 2032. Five-year exploration licences issued in 2022 went to Moana Minerals, Cook Islands Cobalt and Cobalt Seabed Resources, and a 2026 NOAA expedition reported dense nodule fields. A Cook Islands News poll found more than 50% of voters opposed seabed mining, while a local environmental group criticised a new US exploration partner and growing US and Chinese involvement (refs 7, 8).

location.type: Seabed mineral exploration licence areas (national EEZ)
location.detail: Polymetallic nodules at 4,000 to 6,000 m depth across the Cook Islands EEZ, including the Manihiki Plateau; the Seabed Minerals Authority is based in Rarotonga (refs 1, 3).

records.layer_rationale: A national seabed minerals regime is moving from exploration towards a decision on mining in the country's EEZ.

notes.harm: A July 2026 report cited by Cook Islands News warns of unaddressed radioactive-contamination risks, while the Seabed Minerals Authority says there is currently no evidence of severe toxic effects, so harm is potential (ref 5).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery closure or lost income is reported; Cook Islands News says opponents warn of effects on food security and culture (ref 1).
notes.scale: The licences and nodule fields cover the national EEZ, estimated at 6.7 billion tonnes of nodules by Cook Islands News, which is a national-waters issue (ref 1).
notes.duration: Exploration licences date from 2022 and were extended in November 2025 to at least 2032, so the issue is chronic (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The government formally extended exploration and licences remain active, a formal licensing step short of an enforcement order (ref 2).

records.title: Pacific Islands Forum leaders keep a member-led approach to deep-sea minerals as Fiji and French Polynesia press for a pause and civil society warns of sponsor liability
records.description: At their September 2026 meeting in Palau, Forum leaders endorsed a member-led regional approach and a regional repository of deep-sea mineral data, and PINA reports that members still hold differing views. Fiji describes a 10-year precautionary pause on commercial mining in its waters while still licensing exploration, French Polynesia's president called in September 2025 for a regional moratorium, and Cook Islands, Nauru and Tonga are exploring or sponsoring activity. Pacific civil society groups warn that sponsoring states could carry long-term liability.

notes.scale: The debate spans the Forum membership and several Pacific EEZs and territories, a regional-scale issue (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Civil society says it has called for a ban since the 2012 Leaders' Forum, and the first leaders-level Talanoa was held in early 2025 (refs 2, 3).
notes.significance: The 2026 Forum Leaders' Communique formally endorsed a regional approach and repository on deep-sea minerals, a formal regional position (ref 1).

records.title: Pacific tuna stocks are reported healthy, but El Niño, warming-driven stock shifts and surveillance gaps put island access-fee revenue at risk
records.description: The Pacific Islands Forum Fisheries Agency's 2024-25 annual report says skipjack, yellowfin, bigeye and albacore in the Western and Central Pacific are all assessed as not overfished, and that illegal fishing losses have fallen by more than 50% since 2016. The Secretariat of the Pacific Community has warned that overshooting 1.5 degrees C could shift tuna east out of island zones and cut access-fee revenue by up to US$90 million a year, and a strong El Niño is forecast to disrupt fishing into 2027. Only about 15% of tuna caught in the region is processed onshore, and Pacific ministers want more surveillance investment.

notes.harm: No overfishing is reported, so harm is potential: the SPC projects tuna moving out of island EEZs if warming overshoots 1.5 degrees C (refs 1, 3).
notes.livelihoods: The El Niño report notes fishing effort fell in some areas and shifted to the high seas and Kiribati and Tuvalu waters after the FAD ban, with no closure or income loss quantified (ref 4).
notes.scale: The fishery spans the Western and Central Pacific, which produces about 60% of the world's tuna according to PINA (ref 8).
notes.duration: The surveillance and processing challenges are chronic, with illegal-fishing losses tracked since 2016 and new measures adopted in December 2025 (refs 1, 6).
notes.significance: The Forum Fisheries Committee ministers issued a formal communique in July 2026 and WCPFC22 adopted an albacore management procedure in December 2025 (refs 6, 7).

records.description: The Pacific Islands Forum Fisheries Agency's latest Trade and Industry News report says criminal networks are using tuna shipments, fishing vessels and offshore refuelling to move cocaine from South America across the Pacific. It cites packages washing onto reefs in the Marshall Islands and 26 kg on a reef at Mitiaro in the Cook Islands, and a 2.6 tonne seizure in north-west Viti Levu, Fiji, in early 2026. RNZ separately reported a Cook Islands fisherman's account of finding a package on the Mitiaro reef.

notes.scale: The report describes a South Pacific transit route with landfalls from the Marshall Islands to the Cook Islands, a regional-sea scale (ref 1).

records.title: NOAA confirmed mass coral bleaching across Fiji, Tuvalu, Kiribati, Samoa and French Polynesia in the fourth global event, which it now judges ended in mid-2025
records.description: NOAA announced on 15 April 2024 that the world was in its fourth global coral bleaching event and said mass bleaching had been confirmed across large areas of the South Pacific, including Fiji, Tuvalu, Kiribati, Samoa and French Polynesia. In June 2026 NOAA said bleaching-level heat stress ran from early 2023 to mid-2025, reached about 84% of the world's reef area and was documented in at least 83 countries and territories. NOAA's outlook warns that a developing El Niño could bring widespread bleaching back, with the highest probabilities in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific.

notes.scale: NOAA says about 84% of global reef area had bleaching-level heat stress, spanning the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans (ref 2).
notes.duration: Heat stress ran from early 2023 to mid-2025, about two and a half years, according to NOAA (ref 2).
notes.significance: NOAA formally confirmed the fourth global bleaching event on 15 April 2024 and declared it likely ended in June 2026 (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Inquiry into the loss of HMNZS Manawanui off Upolu finds an autopilot error, training gaps and 12 contributing factors, with the wreck still on the reef in April 2025

The final report found 12 contributing factors, including training and qualification gaps and inadequate risk management. As of April 2025 the navy said it had removed diesel and other pollutants and that no decision had been taken on removing the wreck.

records.title: Record North Atlantic sea-surface temperatures and near-basin-wide marine heatwaves in 2023 and 2024
records.description: Copernicus Marine and Mercator Ocean report that the North Atlantic (0 to 60 N) averaged a record 22.91 C in 2024, 0.6 C above the 2023 record, with 98.8% of the basin hit by a marine heatwave. NOAA Climate.gov noted record North Atlantic surface temperatures from March 2023 through mid-2024. In 2025 the eastern North Atlantic again saw record months, while the basin average ranked lower than in 2023 and 2024.

notes.duration: Record surface temperatures ran from March 2023 into mid-2024 (ref 2) and the eastern basin set record months again in 2025, up to eight in a row at some locations (ref 4).
notes.significance: These are agency monitoring reports and press releases with no notice, listing or enforcement attached (refs 1, 4, 5).

records.title: Near-record warm Atlantic main development region fuels Hurricane Beryl to the earliest Category 4 and 5 on record
records.description: NOAA reported that the main development region of the tropical Atlantic was near record warm in late June 2024, with temperatures closer to those typical of mid-September, and Beryl intensified rapidly over it. The National Hurricane Center report records Beryl as the earliest Category 4 (30 June) and Category 5 (2 July) Atlantic hurricane on record, with 35 direct deaths. The storm formed near 8.9 N 39.6 W; its landfalls and damage are recorded in the Caribbean and Gulf records.

location.detail: Beryl formed about 1,200 n mi east of Barbados and became a hurricane near 49.3 W, the farthest east a June Atlantic hurricane had formed in the tropics; coordinates are the best-track position at its first Category 4 intensity.

records.layer_rationale: Record-warm tropical Atlantic surface water acted as the fuel for rapid intensification of an unusually early major hurricane.

notes.harm: The NHC report attributes 35 direct deaths to Beryl, including 3 in Grenada, 8 in St. Vincent and the Grenadines and 14 in the United States (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The NHC report records over $7 billion of property damage in the United States and 99% of buildings damaged on Carriacou, but these impacts fall in the Caribbean and Gulf, so only restrictions are scored here (ref 1).
notes.scale: Climate.gov describes the main development region of the tropical Atlantic as near record warm, a regional-sea extent rather than a single site (ref 2).
notes.duration: Beryl lasted from 28 June to 9 July 2024 and its Category 5 peak was brief (ref 1), although record warmth persisted before and after (ref 3).
notes.significance: NHC issued advisories and the tropical cyclone report certifies records for earliest Category 4 and 5 hurricanes in the Atlantic (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Beryl became the earliest Category 5 hurricane of record in the Atlantic basin, reaching 145 kt at 0600 UTC on 2 July 2024 (NHC Tropical Cyclone Report).

records.title: Subpolar North Atlantic cold blob south of Greenland tied to a weakening Atlantic overturning circulation
records.description: Two 2025 studies attribute the long-term cooling of the subpolar North Atlantic south of Greenland, the "cold blob", to a weakening Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC); a June 2026 Geophysical Research Letters study led by the Potsdam Institute reaches the same conclusion. Fan and co-authors find an atmospheric radiative pathway and ocean heat transport contribute about equally, and Liu and Li estimate AMOC weakening of 1.01 to 2.97 Sverdrups per century over 1900 to 2005. Direct AMOC measurements cover only about 20 years.

location.name: Subpolar gyre south of Greenland
location.type: Open-ocean cooling region (North Atlantic warming hole)
location.detail: The Liu and Li study places the cold zone between 40 N and 65 N south of Greenland, with cooling and freshening to about 3,000 m depth.

records.layer_rationale: A persistent ocean-circulation signal in the surface temperature field that contrasts with global warming.
secondary_drivers: Colder, drier air above the cold blob

notes.harm: The studies describe a risk to the climate system but document no measured ecological or human harm from the cooling itself (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery or coastal restriction is documented in the cited studies or press coverage (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.scale: The cold zone spans 40 N to 65 N south of Greenland and the AMOC is an Atlantic-wide circulation (ref 2).
notes.duration: Earth.com reports the cold spot has persisted for over 100 years, and Fan and co-authors describe cooling over the 20th century (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Peer-reviewed research and press coverage only, with no agency notice or treaty action (refs 1, 2, 3).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Liu and Li estimate the AMOC weakened by 1.01 to 2.97 Sverdrups per century from 1900 to 2005, using temperature and salinity fingerprints (Communications Earth & Environment, per Earth.com).

measures.name: AMOC weakening, 1900 to 2005
measures.note: Range of 1.01 to 2.97 Sv per century estimated from fingerprints in six sea-surface temperature and three salinity datasets and 94 climate models (ref 2).

measures.name: Modelled cooling trend
measures.note: Up to 0.3 C per century in models with a weakening AMOC (ref 2).

trend.note: Euronews (June 2026) describes the blob as the place on Earth that keeps getting colder, citing a study led by the Potsdam Institute (ref 3).

responsible_bodies.name: Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK)

records.public_contact: PIK press office via pik-potsdam.de.
corrective_actions: No management response is documented; the AMOC is monitored by the RAPID array and other observing programmes, which the sources do not detail.

records.title: Canary Islands marine heatwave of 2023: sea temperature 2.3 C above normal through the summer and still above normal at year end
records.description: Spanish Institute of Oceanography data reported in August 2023 showed Canary Islands surface water at 24.32 C on 8 August, 1.56 C above average. A University of Las Palmas de Gran Canaria study presented at the EGU General Assembly 2024 found the heatwave ran from mid-May to late summer 2023, averaged 2.3 C above normal and stayed above normal for the rest of the year. Weak winds are the proposed driver, and the authors note satellite data may understate how deep the anomaly runs.

secondary_drivers: Collapse of wind speeds in May and June 2023

notes.harm: The sources document temperatures and wind anomalies but no mortality, bleaching or other measured harm around the Canaries (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery, tourism or beach restriction is reported in either source (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The anomaly covers the Canary Islands archipelago waters, a national coastline rather than a single site (ref 1).
notes.duration: The heatwave ran from mid-May through the summer of 2023 and temperatures remained above normal for the rest of the year (ref 2).
notes.significance: A press report on IEO monitoring and a conference abstract; no agency notice or listing (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Forty years of Sargasso Sea acidification, warming and oxygen loss at the Bermuda Atlantic Time-series Study site
records.description: The longest sustained ocean acidification record, from the Bermuda Atlantic Time-series Study and Hydrostation S, shows surface pH down by about 0.1 units since 1983, with hydrogen-ion concentration up more than 30%. Surface water warmed by about 1 C, dissolved oxygen fell by 12.5 umol/kg (about 6%), and calcification conditions have become less favourable. The authors report that ocean chemistry in the 2020s is outside the range observed in the 1980s.

location.name: Bermuda Atlantic Time-series Study site
location.detail: BATS is about 80 km south-east of Bermuda in the Sargasso Sea; Hydrostation S is about 25 km south-east of the island.

records.layer_rationale: Long-term carbonate chemistry, oxygen and temperature change in subtropical gyre surface water.

notes.harm: The authors conclude that calcification conditions have become less favourable, a potential effect on calcifiers rather than documented mortality (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The paper reports no fishery or coastal-economy disruption at the site (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The station represents Sargasso Sea and subtropical gyre surface water, a regional sea, with no basin-wide measurement in the paper (ref 1).
notes.duration: The record spans 1983 to 2023, forty years, with no slowing in the rates of change (ref 1).
notes.significance: A peer-reviewed study with an OA-ICC news item, but no notice or treaty action (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Surface ocean pH at BATS decreased by about 0.1 units from 1983 to 2023, with hydrogen-ion concentration up more than 30% (Bates and Johnson 2023).

records.title: Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt sets a record in 2025 and a second-highest year in 2026
records.description: University of South Florida scientists report that 2025 set a record for sargassum across the tropical Atlantic and 2026 ranked second-highest in the satellite record, with the Caribbean and Gulf both at record regional totals in June 2026. NASA Earth Observatory, citing USF, gives June 2026 totals of 3.6 million tonnes in the western Caribbean, 9 million in the eastern Caribbean and 5 million in the Gulf. The cause is still being investigated, with ocean warming and multiple nutrient sources suggested.

location.detail: A near-continuous belt of mats from West Africa across the tropical North Atlantic to the Gulf; the Caribbean and Gulf beachings are recorded in the CAR and GOM findings.

notes.harm: USF and WGCU describe beach inundation and rotting seaweed but give no measured ecological or health harm figure (refs 1, 3).
notes.livelihoods: WGCU reports beaching continued in July 2026 across southeast Florida, the Caribbean and Lesser Antilles, with problems for resorts, officials and beach towns (ref 3).
notes.scale: NASA describes the belt as stretching nearly continuously from West Africa to the Gulf, an Atlantic-wide feature (ref 2).
notes.duration: The bloom began in 2011 and USF says total Atlantic sargassum has more than doubled about every five years since (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: USF and NASA monitoring and a NOAA-funded research programme, but no formal notice or declaration in the cited pages (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Plastic on every one of 46 monitored beaches across Macaronesia, with Canary Islands highest and five new hotspots
records.description: A 2020 to 2023 monitoring study of 46 beaches on 19 islands in four Macaronesian archipelagos found plastic on every beach, with the Canary Islands showing the highest concentrations. Researchers collected 271,203 plastic items in 430 field expeditions and identified five new plastic arrival hotspots. Beaches facing north-west to east received more plastic, which the authors link to the North Atlantic Subtropical Gyre.

notes.harm: Plastic was present on all 46 beaches, averaging 1,760 microplastic items per square metre, but the abstract reports no mortality or health outcome (ref 1).

notes.duration: Seasonal monitoring ran 2020 to 2023 across 430 expeditions, and earlier Azores surveys found the same pattern in 2018 and 2020 (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.significance: A peer-reviewed academic study, with no regulatory notice or treaty action (ref 1).

records.title: North American lobster-gear plastic tags washing up on Faial and Pico beaches in the Azores
records.description: University of the Azores researchers found more than 1,500 items on Faial and Pico beaches between 2017 and 2025, many of them lobster-fishing gear traced by tag numbers to the United States and Canada, more than 3,000 km away. Among legible tags, 63% came from the US and 37% from Canada, and most tags were 7 to 13 years old, the oldest dating from 1983. Marine litter group head Christopher Pham says the pieces entered the sea many years ago and that knowing the origin would let action be taken at source.

records.title: Fuel-oil spill during bunkering at the Port of La Luz closes Telde beaches and triggers a regional marine pollution emergency
records.description: About 3,000 litres of fuel fell into the sea on the evening of 4 September 2024 during a bunkering operation at the Port of Las Palmas, Gran Canaria, and the slick reached Las Palmas and Telde. The Canary Islands government declared a regional-level marine pollution emergency, activated phase 1 of the National Maritime Plan, and five Telde beaches were closed to bathing. Port officials said the source had been stopped and that most of the fuel remained on the two ships involved.

records.title: Bermuda government study finds about 2,130 buildings at risk from sea level rise and storm surge, after Hurricane Ernesto
records.description: Bermuda's Minister of Home Affairs told the House of Assembly in November 2024 that the Smith Warner International study "Bermuda and Climate Change: Impacts from Sea Level Rise and Changing Storm Activity" found about 2,130 buildings (roughly 6%) at some level of risk, 326 of them highly exposed, and that 96% of coastal reserves require protection. Hurricane Ernesto struck in August 2024 with a dangerous storm surge, leaving about 26,100 of 36,000 utility customers without power. The government will create an expanded climate task force and a National Action Plan.

records.title: Azores 30% marine protected area network takes effect after a vote to keep fishing out of the fully protected half
records.description: The Azores Marine Protected Areas Network, approved in October 2024 and in force from 1 January 2026, covers about 287,000 km2, or 30% of Azorean waters, split between fully and highly protected areas. On 15 January 2026 the regional parliament kept the ban on all fishing in the fully protected areas but allowed tuna pole-and-line fishing in highly protected areas. The Azores Fisheries Federation says it is disappointed and that EUR 10 million of compensation falls short of the sector's annual revenue of EUR 42 million.

notes.livelihoods: Fishing is banned in the fully protected half and restricted in the highly protected half; the Fisheries Federation says compensation of EUR 10 million over three years falls short of EUR 42 million in annual sector revenue (ref 1).

notes.significance: A regional law is in force since 1 January 2026 and parliament voted on 15 January 2026 to uphold the no-fishing rule (ref 1).

records.title: Bermuda and the UK draft the Hamilton II Declaration to seek high seas protection for the Sargasso Sea under the new High Seas Treaty
records.description: The Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ) Agreement entered into force on 17 January 2026. Bermuda and the UK held a civil society consultation on 20 March 2026 on a draft Hamilton II Declaration that would build political support for a collective proposal to protect the Sargasso Sea's high seas areas, ahead of the first Conference of the Parties due before 17 January 2027. In a House of Lords debate on 6 July 2026 the UK minister said the measures still need to be negotiated and did not commit to the highest level of protection.

records.title: Ship collisions push Canary Islands sperm whales toward local extinction, researchers warn
records.description: In May 2025 researchers at the Canary Islands Oceanographic Centre (IEO-CSIC) and the University of La Laguna said two more sperm whales had died after ship strikes off Tenerife and that ship collisions are driving the species toward local extinction; they report that abundance has roughly halved. records.title: NAMMCO advises zero catch of narwhal and beluga in East Greenland after quotas diverged from earlier advice
records.description: At its meeting in Nuuk on 24 to 26 March 2026, the North Atlantic Marine Mammal Commission endorsed its Scientific Committee's advice for a zero-catch limit for narwhal and beluga in East Greenland, citing a small narwhal stock and low beluga numbers. In 2022 Polar Journal reported that the Greenland government set 2023 quotas of 50 narwhals and 30 belugas for the east coast, different from NAMMCO's recommendation of a longer hunting pause. records.title: Portugal enacts a seabed mining moratorium to 2050 while three ISA exploration contracts cover the Mid-Atlantic Ridge

records.title: Critically endangered angelshark depends on the Canary Islands as its stronghold while a fisheries decree is drafted
records.description: The Angel Shark Project says the Canary Islands are the critically endangered angelshark's unique stronghold in Europe, where it has been on the Spanish endangered species list for Canary waters since 2019. Its January to March 2025 report counts 277 reported angelsharks on all eight islands, including the largest recorded aggregation, over 60 animals off Fuerteventura. The project asked to take part in public consultation on a new Canary fisheries decree and flagged recreational fishing impacts. The outcome of the consultation was not found.

location.name: Canary Islands angelshark habitat
location.detail: Eight islands; confirmed nursery at Las Teresitas, Tenerife; aggregation off Fuerteventura

records.layer_rationale: A critically endangered shark with a restricted stronghold faces bycatch and recreational fishing pressure.

notes.harm: The project lists incidental catch by recreational, charter and commercial fishers and habitat degradation as threats (ref 1); no mortality count is given.
notes.livelihoods: No fishing closure is documented; the project proposes protection measures in the fisheries decree (ref 2).
notes.scale: The species is reported on all eight islands in the archipelago (ref 2).
notes.duration: The species was listed in 2019 and an action plan dates from 2016, so the threats are chronic (ref 1).
notes.significance: A 2019 listing in the Spanish endangered species catalogue as "in danger of extinction" prohibits killing, capture and disturbance in Canary waters (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: 277 angelsharks were reported across all eight Canary Islands in January to March 2025, including a record aggregation of over 60 off Fuerteventura.

measures.note: Angel Shark Project quarterly report (ref 2); sightings by divers, not a population count.

measures.note: More than 60, Fuerteventura (ref 2).

records.title: Sea Lion oil field north of the Falklands reaches final investment decision after a contested environmental review
records.description: Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration took a final investment decision on the Sea Lion field in December 2025, after the Falkland Islands Government approved the field development and production programme. Phase 1 plans 11 subsea wells tied to a redeployed FPSO with first oil targeted for 2028. Falklands Conservation told the 2024 environmental consultation that the Environmental Impact Statement was not fit for purpose, citing carbon offsets, wildlife data gaps and spill and decommissioning risk.

location.detail: About 220 km north of the Falkland Islands, licences PL032 and PL004b, Falkland Islands (Malvinas) waters.

records.layer_rationale: A new offshore hydrocarbon development whose approval, financing and environmental review are the documented issue.

notes.harm: Falklands Conservation says the EIS leaves 9 million tonnes of development emissions and over 100 million tonnes from burning the oil unoffset and has over 100 errors or omissions in two sections reviewed (ref 5); no harm has yet occurred.
notes.livelihoods: No restriction or closure is reported in the sources; the Planning and Building Committee approved 160 worker housing units, 320 beds, for the field (ref 6).
notes.scale: A single licensed field about 220 km north of the islands (ref 4), so site-level.
notes.duration: The project is planned to produce for over 30 years (ref 4) with first oil in 2028 (ref 1), a chronic exposure.
notes.significance: The Falkland Islands Government approved the field development and production programme, moving the licences into a 35-year exploitation phase (refs 2, 3).

records.title: Argentina announces sanctions bill against oil companies and suppliers working around the Falklands
records.description: On 3 September 2026 Argentine President Javier Milei said he would send Congress a "national sovereignty defence" bill raising penalties for operating around the Falkland Islands without Argentine authorisation, extending sanctions to suppliers, shareholders and directors. The move targets the Sea Lion project. The UK government replied that the islanders have the right to exploit their own natural resources. Argentina separately does not recognise the Falklands fisheries conservation zone, so the two sides manage shared stocks separately.

location.detail: Waters around the Falkland Islands and the Sea Lion licence area north of the islands; Argentina-UK sovereignty dispute.

records.layer_rationale: A sovereignty dispute turned into proposed sanctions affecting offshore energy and fisheries activity.

notes.harm: No environmental or human harm is attributed to the dispute in the cited reports (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: The bill would bring suppliers, shareholders and directors of companies working on Sea Lion within sanctions (ref 1), a potential restriction on the oil project and its contractors.
notes.scale: The dispute covers the Falklands maritime zone as a whole, including fisheries management that Argentina and the islands run separately (ref 2).
notes.duration: The dispute is long-running; the 2013 referendum result and the continuing refusal to recognise the Falklands conservation zone are cited (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: A head-of-state televised announcement of a bill on 3 September 2026 (ref 1); a proposal, not yet an enacted law.

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Milei said he would send Congress an urgent "national sovereignty defence" bill with penalties applying to companies, shareholders, directors and suppliers (ref 1).

records.title: Hundreds of distant-water squid jiggers fish the unregulated high seas at Argentina's mile 201 edge
records.description: Reports from 2025 and 2026 describe 300 to 600 foreign vessels, mainly Chinese, Korean and Taiwanese, fishing Illex squid just outside Argentina's 200-mile zone with no catch limits. The Environmental Justice Foundation found Chinese fishing hours rose 85% between 2019 and 2024 and that pressure outside the zone is over four times that inside it, alongside labour abuses on board. Argentine and Spanish industry voices warn of stock collapse.

location.name: Mile 201, high seas beyond Argentina's EEZ
location.detail: High seas of the south-west Atlantic along the outer edge of the Argentine 200-nautical-mile zone; the Argentine EEZ itself is covered under BRA.

records.layer_rationale: Intensive unregulated fishing of a keystone squid stock on the high seas.

notes.harm: EJF testimonies from 169 workers report up to five deaths aboard four Chinese vessels, beatings and 14 to 18 hour days, and crews describing the deliberate killing of South American fur seals (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: Argentine industry and Spanish shipowners warn that high-seas fishing could deplete Illex and depress prices; no formal closure exists (refs 4, 5).
notes.scale: The fleet works the outer edge of the Argentine zone across the south-west Atlantic, a regional sea (refs 3, 4).
notes.duration: The foreign fleet operates five or six months a year (ref 3) with effort rising 2019 to 2024 and reports repeated in 2025 and 2026 (refs 1, 4, 5).
notes.significance: Only NGO reports, industry statements and Argentine naval monitoring are cited; no regional fisheries body or enforcement order covers these waters (refs 1, 3).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Chinese squid vessels' fishing hours rose 85% between 2019 and 2024 (EJF, ref 1); about 343 vessels operate each year just outside the zone (ref 2).

measures.name: Vessels fishing just outside the Argentine zone
measures.note: EJF report as reported by MercoPress, 18 Sep 2025 (ref 2); other sources give 300 to 500 (ref 5) and 400 to 600 (ref 4).

measures.name: Growth in Chinese squid fishing hours 2019 to 2024
measures.note: EJF via Oceanographic, 17 Sep 2025 (ref 1).

measures.name: Fishing pressure outside vs inside the Argentine zone
measures.note: Oceanographic reports pressure over four times greater than in adjacent regulated Argentine waters (ref 1).

measures.note: MercoPress cites 1.5 to 3 million tonnes for Asian fleets on the high seas (ref 5) and the same range for the whole south-west Atlantic (ref 4); a wide range, not one reported value.

signals: Argentine shortfin squid supported 12.2% of the global squid catch in 2023 (ref 1).
Spanish shipowners warn of lower prices and a depleted resource (ref 5).

trend.note: Fishing effort rose 65% to 85% between 2019 and 2024 depending on the measure (refs 1, 3, 4).

records.title: Falklands Loligo squid seasons closed early for a third straight year as biomass falls, and Illex catch drops
records.description: The Falklands Fisheries Department closed the 2025 winter Loligo season after biomass estimates fell from 29,735 to 14,722 tonnes, and in August 2026 closed the second season again three days after a two-week pause, calling biomass "very low". The Illex season ended on 22 June 2026 with catches about 30% below the ten-year average. Officials cite squid movements out of the area, rising hake predation and heavier fishing power.

location.name: Loligo Box and Falklands Conservation Zone
location.detail: Falkland Islands fishing zones: the Loligo Box north-east of the islands and the Illex grounds, Falkland Islands (Malvinas) waters.

records.layer_rationale: Declining squid stocks and repeated season closures in a managed fishery.

notes.harm: The winter 2025 Loligo biomass estimate fell from 29,735 to 21,695 and then 14,722 tonnes with a lower bound of 6,539 tonnes (refs 2, 3).
notes.livelihoods: Closures hit 16 Spanish-Falklands joint-venture freezer trawlers in 2026 (ref 8) and the 2025 first season catch reached about 22,000 tonnes against a normal 30,000 (ref 1).
notes.scale: The closures apply to the Falklands Loligo Box and one national fishery rather than a whole sea (refs 3, 7).
notes.duration: The second season never opened in 2024 and was closed in 2025 and 2026, the fourth consecutive year of second-season difficulty (ref 7).
notes.significance: The Fisheries Department issued formal closure notices, including one dated 6 August 2025 (ref 3).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Winter 2025 Loligo biomass estimate fell to 14,722 tonnes (lower confidence bound 6,539 tonnes) after early catches dropped quickly (refs 2, 3).

records.title: H5N1 avian flu kills penguin chicks and adults on Falklands colonies and keeps recurring
records.description: In January 2024 the Falkland Islands Government confirmed H5N1 in gentoo penguins on Sea Lion Island, with more than 200 chicks and some adults found dead and Steeple Jason also closed. Operator pages updated in July 2026 report that a small number of cases have been recorded since late 2023 and that most landing sites remain open with biosecurity rules.

notes.harm: More than 200 penguin chicks and some adults were found dead on Sea Lion Island by 31 Jan 2024, and the government said many more were dying (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Sea Lion Island was closed to visitors from 19 January 2024 and Steeple Jason was also closed (ref 1); cruise biosecurity rules persist (ref 4).
notes.scale: Confirmed on one island group, with sample results pending from a second, so site to local level (refs 1, 3).
notes.duration: Cases have recurred since late 2023 through at least July 2026 (ref 4).
notes.significance: The Falkland Islands Government confirmed H5N1 and closed sites, a formal advisory action (refs 1, 3).

records.title: Plastic rocks and microplastics bury green turtle nesting beaches on Trindade island
records.description: A 2026 Marine Pollution Bulletin study of Trindade, a Brazilian oceanic island, found that plastic rocks first seen in 2019 have lost about 40% of their size and spread fragments to six more beaches, and that plastic accumulates up to 10 cm deep in green turtle nest depressions. The researchers trace the plastic to fishing and shipping debris and fires over beach litter.

notes.livelihoods: No fishery, route or beach restriction is reported; the only human presence is a navy detachment of 30 to 40 (ref 1).
notes.scale: The findings concern one island, with fragments spread across six further beaches (ref 1).
notes.duration: The plastic rocks were first seen in 2019 and were monitored for five years (ref 1), and the 2023 report shows the same problem (ref 2).
notes.significance: A peer-reviewed study and press coverage, with no formal notice or listing (refs 1, 2).

records.title: South Atlantic among the fastest-warming ocean regions as ocean heat content sets a 2025 record
records.description: A multi-institution analysis in Advances in Atmospheric Sciences found the ocean absorbed about 23 zettajoules in 2025, a record, with the tropical and South Atlantic among the regions of most extreme warming. Mercator Ocean's bulletin of 22 November 2025 also flagged a developing moderate-to-strong marine heatwave in the centre of the basin near 40 degrees south.

records.title: Gough Island mouse eradication failed in 2021, leaving seabird chicks and albatrosses under predation
records.description: The 2021 helicopter bait drop on Gough Island did not remove every house mouse: a mouse was caught on camera in December 2021 and four more were caught later, and the programme stated it had not met its primary objective. Mice have been estimated to kill about two million seabird chicks a year, and only 21 MacGillivray's prion chicks fledged from about 370 monitored nests between 2014 and 2021.

notes.duration: Mice have preyed on the colony since their 19th-century introduction, and live mice were confirmed in 2022 after the failed eradication (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The conservation programme publicly reported the eradication had not met its main goal, an operator statement and not a regulatory action (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Longliner Argos Georgia founders east of the Falklands with 13 dead after a hatch failure

records.title: Falklands weighs large-scale salmon farming in its waters amid public pushback
records.description: The Falkland Islands Government began scoping large-scale commercial salmon farming in November 2024, with 55 responses, and published consultation documents on 29 June 2026, with an online survey open until 30 October 2026. Campaign group Salmon Free Falklands cites pollution, sea lice, escapes and chemical use from the Faroe Islands and questions farming a non-native species.

location.name: Falkland Islands waters
location.detail: Falkland Islands (Malvinas) waters; no site is specified in the cited sources.

records.layer_rationale: A policy decision on whether to allow industrial finfish farming.

notes.harm: Salmon Free Falklands cites Faroese fjords too polluted by farm effluent for further farming, and lice, escapes, plastic debris and chemicals (ref 3); no Falklands farm exists.
notes.livelihoods: No disruption is reported; the consultation concerns future licensing (refs 1, 4).

records.title: Antarctic sea ice stays far below average from 2022 to 2026, with record-low daily extents reported in October 2026
records.description: NSIDC reports that the four lowest annual Antarctic sea-ice minimums on record all fell in 2022 to 2025, that the 2025 and provisional 2026 winter maximums were each the third lowest, and that daily extent has been at record lows since 2 October 2026. The February 2026 minimum was close to average, and a 2025 peer-reviewed study argues that a regime shift in Antarctic sea ice began in 2017, while NSIDC says the 2025 downward trend is not statistically significant.

records.title: Record August 2025 sea surface temperatures in the Kara Sea and up to 7 C above normal across Arctic Atlantic-sector seas
records.description: NOAA's Arctic Report Card essay on sea surface temperature reports that the Arctic Ocean's mean August 2025 temperature was the second warmest on record, behind only August 2007, and that Kara Sea values were the warmest on record for the month. Parts of the Barents, Kara and Laptev seas ran roughly 1 to 4 C above the 1991-2020 mean, with local anomalies near 7 C. The authors note that Arctic marine heatwaves are a concern for already stressed ecosystems and that warming surface waters accelerate sea-ice loss.

notes.scale: The strongest anomalies sit in the Barents, Kara and Laptev seas, a regional sector rather than the whole Arctic Ocean, where Chukchi and Beaufort parts were cooler than normal (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Trends since 1982 are statistically significant for the Kara (0.12 C per year), Laptev (0.08) and Barents (0.06) seas, so the warming is chronic rather than a single month (ref 1).

records.title: Severe marine heatwave and record daily sea surface temperature in the Norwegian Sea, July 2025
records.description: Copernicus's European State of the Climate 2025 ocean chapter reports severe marine heatwave conditions in the Norwegian Sea from mid-July to early August 2025. On 24 to 25 July the daily average sea surface temperature over the sea reached a record 15.5 C, with a 3 C anomaly that was the largest daily anomaly recorded for the sector in any month. Record monthly sea surface temperatures also became more widespread across the Norwegian, Greenland and Barents seas in the second half of 2025.

records.title: Atlantification now reaches the central Arctic Ocean, weakening the halocline that shielded sea ice from ocean heat
records.description: NOAA's Arctic Report Card 2025 essay by Polyakov, Ingvaldsen and Bluhm reports that an influx of warmer, saltier Atlantic water and biota now reaches the central Arctic Ocean, with a signal in the western Amerasian Basin moving toward Alaska. In the eastern Eurasian Basin the Atlantic Water layer has shoaled from about 150 m in the early 2000s to as shallow as 70 m, and sea-ice thinning linked to the process spans the central Arctic. The essay suggests the Atlantic water entering the Arctic from the Barents Sea has warmed more strongly than that through Fram Strait.

notes.significance: The essay is a scientific assessment without a regulatory, treaty or court action attached (ref 1).

records.title: Tuktoyaktuk shoreline erosion threatens the harbour barrier, with C$53.7 million of federal protection and homes moved inland
records.description: Tuktoyaktuk, a hamlet on the Beaufort Sea coast, is losing shoreline to storm waves and thawing permafrost. In July 2023 the federal government said it would spend about C$53.7 million on rock armour for the most-eroded shoreline and in front of Tuktoyaktuk Island, which shields the harbour, and researchers then expected the island to be breached in 20 to 25 years. A 2025 Arctic Inspiration Prize report says the island eroded 2 m in a year, forced three homes to be moved to higher ground, and could be breached in 18 to 20 years.

records.title: Greenland ice sheet and Arctic glaciers keep adding to global sea level rise in the 2024-25 season
records.description: NOAA's Arctic Report Card 2025 reports that the Greenland Ice Sheet lost 129 Gt of ice in the 2025 mass balance year (September 2024 to August 2025), less than the 2003-24 average loss of 219 Gt but part of net loss every year since the late 1990s. Arctic glaciers and ice caps outside Greenland lost 151 Gt in 2023/24, adding about 0.42 mm to sea level, and Svalbard glaciers had severe losses. records.title: Aragonite-undersaturated water thickens in the Canada Basin, the open-ocean region most susceptible to acidification
records.description: A 2025 study in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Oceans found that aragonite-undersaturated water in the Canada Basin thickened from none at the surface in 2003 to 19 m in 2019, and from 94 m to 136 m in the subsurface layer. The undersaturated share of the 0 to 250 m water column rose from 38% to 62%. The authors say surface thickening was driven by freshening until 2012 and by anthropogenic CO2 uptake after 2012, and warn that a weaker Beaufort Gyre could bring undersaturated water shallower, potentially affecting marine life.

records.title: Microplastic fluxes recorded over 21 months at the HAUSGARTEN observatory in Fram Strait, with high levels in sea-ice algae
records.description: An Alfred Wegener Institute study published online in December 2024 measured microplastics in sediment traps at the HAUSGARTEN observatory in Fram Strait from September 2019 to July 2021. Fluxes ranged from 0 to 2.9 particles per square metre per day, peaked in April 2020 and April 2021, and all particles were under 300 micrometres. records.title: Plastic dominates litter on Svalbard beaches, with debris traced to more than 25 countries
records.description: Alfred Wegener Institute researchers working with expedition-cruise tourists collected more than 23,000 items weighing 1,620 kg on 14 remote Spitsbergen beaches between 2016 and 2021, about 80% of it plastic. records.title: Sunken nuclear submarines K-27 and K-159 remain on the Kara and Barents Sea floors as Russia funds a lifting plan
records.description: Two Soviet nuclear submarines lie on the Arctic seabed: K-27, scuttled in Stepovoy Bay off Novaya Zemlya in the Kara Sea, and K-159, which sank in the Barents Sea in 2003 with about 800 kg of spent nuclear fuel. The Barents Observer reported on 20 October 2025 that Russia's draft 2026 budget and 2027-2028 plan include about 30 billion rubles for planning and lifting them, with preparations in 2026 and funding from 2027. Bellona, on 4 November 2025, judged raising them in the foreseeable future highly improbable and said no concrete plan is public.

records.title: Cargo ship Ruby with 20,000 tonnes of ammonium nitrate sheltered off Tromsø in September 2024
records.description: The Maltese-flagged cargo ship Ruby, carrying 20,000 tons of ammonium nitrate from Kandalaksha, Russia, bound for Las Palmas, asked Norway for shelter on 26 August 2024 because of storms and anchored near Vannoya. It then docked at Breivika in Tromsø, where police ordered it to leave, and on 4 September 2024 it departed with two tugs to anchor about 30 nautical miles north of the city. The captain reported slight hull, propeller and rudder damage, and the Barents Observer reported its future was uncertain.

records.title: IMO Arctic heavy fuel oil ban in force since July 2024 but waivers and exemptions allow continued use until 2029
records.description: IMO's MARPOL Annex I regulation 43A bans the use and carriage of heavy fuel oil as fuel by ships in Arctic waters from 1 July 2024, but ships with protected fuel tanks are exempt and Arctic coastal states can waive the rule for their flagged ships until 1 July 2029. The Clean Arctic Alliance, citing ICCT analysis, says 74% of Arctic shipping can continue as before and that HFO use and carriage may rise between 2024 and 2029. Russia told the IMO the amendments would not enter into force for it, and Canada said it intends to comply.

notes.livelihoods: The sources report no fishery or route restriction; the ban itself restricts a fuel type (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The rule covers all IMO-defined Arctic waters, a basin-scale regime (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Waivers run from July 2024 to July 2029, a multi-year period (refs 1, 3).

records.description: On 9 January 2024 the Storting approved opening about 281,200 km2 of Norwegian Arctic seabed to exploration for seabed minerals, per the European Parliament's summary. The European Parliament called for a moratorium on 7 February 2024, and WWF-Norway notified the government in April 2024 that it would take legal action, arguing the strategic impact assessment fell short of legal minimums. In early December 2025 a budget agreement dropped the first licensing round, and Parliament voted on the pause on 5 December 2025; Mongabay reports no round before 2029 while the Energy Ministry says its policy and regulatory framework are unchanged.

records.title: Svalbard seabirds in decline: Brunnich's guillemot, ivory gull and kittiwake monitoring to May 2026

records.description: The Arctic Council's official meetings have been paused since March 2022 and its working groups resumed virtual meetings in 2024 with Russia taking part, Arctic Today reported in June 2026. Russia stopped paying its Council dues in 2024, per the same report. Denmark took the chair from Norway in May 2025 and Sweden follows in 2027; Denmark's ambassador said the Council is 'not back to what it used to be. But it's not dead either.'

location.name: Arctic Council
location.detail: Eight Arctic states and Indigenous permanent participants; Denmark (with Greenland) chairs 2025 to 2027.

records.layer_rationale: A regional governance body whose consensus-based work on the Arctic marine environment is constrained by the Russia split.

notes.harm: No ecological harm is documented; the sources describe a governance constraint (refs 1 to 3).
notes.livelihoods: No livelihood disruption is documented in the sources.
notes.scale: The Council covers the whole circumpolar Arctic and its marine working groups (ref 1).
notes.duration: Official meetings have been paused since March 2022, over four years (ref 1).
notes.significance: The seven Western members suspended Council work and partially resumed projects without Russia in June 2022 (ref 3); Russia stopped paying dues in 2024 (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Arctic Council official meetings have been paused since March 2022 while working groups meet virtually with all eight states, including Russia (Arctic Today, ref 1).

measures.note: Arctic Today, June 2026 (ref 1).

measures.name: Years of paused official meetings

corrective_actions: Working groups resumed virtual meetings in 2024; Denmark's chairship holds smaller strategic planning consultations (ref 1).
