records.title: Russia accuses Norway of militarizing Svalbard (March 2025) amid longstanding disputes over Svalbard Treaty rights and marine protection zones
records.description: On 14 March 2025 Russia summoned Norway's ambassador, accusing Norway of militarizing Svalbard, which Norway denied, saying Svalbard is part of Norway and NATO and Norway acts in line with the 1920 treaty, Reuters reported. A 2020 Russian letter, reported by High North News, objected to Norway's fish protection zone around Svalbard and to nature protection zones that it said limit economic activity. Russia keeps two settlements, Barentsburg and Pyramiden, with about 340 residents.

location.name: Svalbard
location.detail: Norwegian archipelago in the Barents and Greenland Seas; Russian settlements Barentsburg and Pyramiden.

records.layer_rationale: A treaty dispute over Svalbard's regime including its fish protection zone and nature protection areas.

notes.harm: No environmental harm is documented; the sources describe a diplomatic dispute (refs 1, 3).
notes.livelihoods: Russia objects to limits on its economic activity, a helicopter restriction and deportation procedures, but no disruption is quantified (ref 3).
notes.scale: The dispute concerns the Svalbard archipelago and its waters (ref 1).
notes.duration: Russian objections date from a February 2020 letter and recurred in March 2025 (refs 1, 3).
notes.significance: Russia summoned Norway's ambassador on 14 March 2025, a formal diplomatic step (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Russia's foreign ministry urged Norway to renounce activity that 'undermines the international legal foundations' of Svalbard's regime (Reuters, 14 March 2025, ref 1).

measures.name: Residents of Russian settlements
measures.note: Out of 2,945 Svalbard residents per Statistics Norway, cited by Reuters (ref 1).

trend.note: Two dated Russian complaints (2020, 2025) were read; no trend can be drawn from them.

records.public_contact: Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, published general contact channels at regjeringen.no.
corrective_actions: Norway's foreign ministry says all activities on Svalbard must follow Norwegian law (ref 3).

records.title: Western Hudson Bay polar bears: 2021 survey counted 618 bears, down from 842 in 2016, as harvest consultations continued in 2024
records.description: A Government of Nunavut aerial survey in 2021 estimated 618 polar bears in Western Hudson Bay, against 842 in 2016, a 27% decline; an Associated Press report said bears there continue to die in high numbers, with females and cubs hit hardest. Nunavut's Department of Environment says that when Western and Southern Hudson Bay are pooled the difference between 2016 and 2021 was one bear, and that part of the decline reflects movement across the subpopulation boundary. It recommended keeping the harvest limit at 38 bears a year in 2024 and hunters' organizations asked for an increase.

location.name: Western Hudson Bay polar bear subpopulation
location.detail: Hudson Bay coast of Manitoba and Nunavut, including the Churchill area; harvest by Arviat, Whale Cove and Rankin Inlet.

records.layer_rationale: A sea-ice-dependent marine mammal subpopulation with a contested decline and a managed harvest.

notes.harm: The 2021 survey estimated 618 bears against 842 in 2016, but Nunavut says pooled Western and Southern Hudson Bay estimates differed by one bear (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: A total allowable harvest of 38 bears a year applies and hunters' organizations did not support the recommendation, asking for an increase (ref 1).
notes.scale: The finding concerns a single subpopulation (ref 1).
notes.duration: Surveys from 2011 to 2021 show a long decline, with 949 or 1,030 bears in 2011 depending on the source (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The Nunavut Wildlife Management Board put the 2021 survey and harvest recommendation on its formal agenda for 30 October 2024 (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: The 2021 Western Hudson Bay survey estimated 618 bears against 842 in 2016 (AP, ref 2; Nunavut Wildlife Management Board agenda, ref 1).

records.title: Greenland cuts its shrimp quota to 83,125 tonnes, beyond the management plan's 12.5% limit, citing stock concern
records.description: Greenland's government reduced the shrimp quota to 83,125 tonnes, going beyond the 12.5% annual variation the management plan allows, High North News reported on 4 December 2024 from Sermitsiaq. The government said the cut keeps catches at a level for long-term use of the stock. Shrimp exports were worth about 2 billion kroner from January to October 2024, around half of Greenland's exports.

location.name: West Greenland shrimp fishery
location.detail: Greenland's waters; the cited report does not name the fishing areas.

records.layer_rationale: A stock-concern quota reduction affecting Greenland's main export fishery.

notes.harm: The government cited concern for the stock; no biomass figure was reported (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The quota cut applies to a fishery worth about 2 billion kroner of Greenland's roughly 4 billion kroner of exports from January to October 2024 (ref 1).
notes.scale: A single stock under national management (ref 1).
notes.duration: One quota decision, reported December 2024; a Polar Seafood lawsuit over a halibut quota reallocation was reported in June 2025 as related context (ref 2).
notes.significance: A formal government decision exceeded the management plan's 12.5% variation limit (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Greenland keeps its 2021 halt on new oil and gas exploration licences as outside interest is reported in 2026
records.description: In July 2021 Greenland's government announced it would stop issuing new licences for oil and gas exploration, citing climate and environmental concerns and cost, and said the step protects nature, fisheries and tourism. IBTimes UK reported in August 2026 on an unnamed company it described as linked to Donald Trump, quoting Greenlandic officials that no drilling can take place without official approval and that Greenland keeps full authority over natural resource decisions. The report says prospects for new oil drilling remain highly limited.

location.name: Greenland offshore and onshore petroleum licensing
location.detail: Greenland's waters and territory; the cited sources do not locate specific licence blocks.

records.layer_rationale: A national moratorium on new licences, with reported foreign interest testing it.

notes.harm: No drilling harm is documented; the sources describe a licensing policy (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: No livelihood disruption is documented; the 2021 decision cited protection of fisheries and tourism (ref 1).
notes.scale: The policy applies to Greenland's national waters and territory (ref 1).
notes.duration: The halt dates from July 2021 and was still described as in force in August 2026, over five years (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: A government decision halts new licences, and officials said in August 2026 that no drilling can take place without approval (refs 1, 2).
